The wrong pair is (4) Dr Mohan Rao - polio.

The chapter connects Dr Mohan Rao with the kidney transplant, not with polio. Such surgeries were not common in India till 1971, but in that year Dr Johny and Dr Mohan Rao successfully transplanted a kidney donated by a living person into a patient's body at the Christian Medical College hospital at Vellore in Tamil Nadu. Polio is not linked to any doctor's name in the chapter; it was brought under control by the 'pulse polio' immunisation programme started in 1995.

The other three pairs are correct. Dr N. Gopinath led the first successful open heart surgery in 1962, Ramchandra Sharma was the skilled craftsman who helped make the artificial limbs of the Jaipur foot, and the test-tube baby experiment was successfully carried out under the supervision of Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyaya.

The chapter's own text spells this doctor's name 'Dr N. Gopinath', while the exercise prints it as 'Dr N Gopinathan'; the same person is meant in both places.

During the pre-independence period, the institution of the family was an important identifying feature of Indian society, and India was known all over the world as the country of joint families. In the joint family, priority was given to the head of the family and to the family as an institution rather than to the individual, and a larger proportion of vocations ran in the family. The provisions of the Constitution shook the foundations of the caste system and helped to make the practice of vocations running in the family obsolete. The wave of globalisation has now given an impetus to the system of nuclear families, in which the family becomes secondary and priority is given to individuals. This trend towards nuclear families is seen mainly in the urban community, while the joint family system continued longer in the rural community.

The invention of the 'Jaipur Foot' has transformed the lives of the disabled in India. Before 1968, if a person lost a leg in an accident, he had to suffer for the rest of his life. In order to remedy this situation, Dr Pramod Sethi designed and manufactured artificial limbs, noses and ears with the help of the skilled craftsman Ramchandra Sharma. The artificial body parts made with the Jaipur foot technology have made it easy for the differently abled to walk bare-foot on rough surfaces, run, go cycling, work in the fields, climb trees and even climb mountains. They also save the expense of shoes, since no footwear is needed on these artificial limbs, and the legs can be bent at the knees so that the person can sit cross-legged. These feet are convenient while working in water or in wet conditions as well.

Urbanisation is a process of the concentration of population in a city or urban area. Increasing population is one major reason for urbanisation, and a few other factors affecting it are air, water and the economic as well as social organisations that are necessary for community life. In the context of post-independence India, the increase in urban population is also due to the reduction in the mortality rate, industrialisation, the unavailability of means of livelihood in rural areas, job opportunities in cities and the migration that results from this. This puts a strain on the cities. To reduce that strain it is necessary to make jobs available in villages, to achieve a balance in economic development, to control the expansion of metros and to provide the necessary services and facilities in both the urban as well as the rural areas.

Earlier, every village was economically self-sufficient. A majority of the villagers were dependent on farming, and the farm produce used to be distributed among the artisans as payment for their work. Now this situation has changed. Rural areas are engaged in agriculture and in occupations ancillary to farming, while urban society is engaged in non-agricultural production and in the service sector. Before globalisation, the rural community had elementary kinds of vocations and tended to send villagers to the cities, whereas the urban community had large industries, produced for global consumption and accommodated outsiders.

The Constitution of India states that the primary duty of the government is to raise the people's standard of living, to ensure proper nutrition and to improve public health. The condition of infants made this duty urgent: before 1978, every year six Indian infants out of every ten who were born faced fatal health problems in the very first year of their birth. The immunisation programme was therefore taken up to overcome the threat of polio, measles, tetanus, TB, diphtheria and whooping cough. To deal with polio in particular, the 'pulse polio' immunisation programme was started in 1995, and it has controlled polio.

One of the three major challenges of rural development is developing facilities to meet social needs, and among these, priority has to be given to facilities for public hygiene and health-care. Even today the rural population faces problems related to the year round provision of drinking water, along with toilets, open drainage, narrow roads, inadequate electrification and a lack of facilities for medical treatment. Because drinking water was not available in villages throughout the year, the State of Maharashtra started the 'Rural Water Supply Scheme' for sinking wells and providing piped water. This was done under the collective development scheme, which had an important place in all the first four five year plans of the government of India. By 1971, 1677 small dams had also been built in the State.

According to our Constitution, all Indians are equal before the law, and they cannot be discriminated against on the basis of religion, race, caste, gender or place of birth. Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar brought about a sea change in our traditional mindset, and he brought it about through the medium of the Indian Constitution. Along with this equality, all citizens have the right to freedom of speech and expression, the freedom to assemble peacefully without arms and the freedom to form associations. They also have the freedom to move, to live and settle down anywhere on Indian territory and to practise any occupation. Indian citizens living anywhere in India enjoy the right to nurture their language, script and culture. These provisions in the Constitution shook the foundations of the caste system, and they helped to make the practice of vocations running in the family obsolete. Thus began a series of minor and major changes in society: now anyone can go into a restaurant irrespective of his religion, race, caste or gender, and boards welcoming all are seen outside restaurants. Another very significant change of the post-independence period is the right to express opinions against the government, because earlier there were limits on expressing any opinion against political rulers, and now citizens can register their protest against the policies of the government through newspapers, speeches or other media.

The objective of establishing the welfare state has been incorporated in the Constitution itself, and India is the first country in the world to do so. The social welfare programmes aim to make opportunities for full-time employment, health care, education and development available to all Indian citizens. This aim is important because Indian society is riddled with large scale economic, social, educational and cultural inequalities. It is therefore necessary that opportunities for development reach women, children, the differently abled, the scheduled castes and tribes as well as other minorities. This was the greatest challenge facing the government during the post-independence period. That is why, on 14th June 1964, the government of India constituted the Ministry of Social Welfare, and a similar arrangement exists at the state level too. Under this ministry various programmes are implemented for nutrition and child-development, social security and social protection, and women's welfare and development. According to the 1971 Census, 22% of the people in India belonged to the scheduled castes and tribes, so laws were enacted so that they got educational scholarships and representation in Parliament as well as the State Assemblies, and some seats are also reserved for them in government services.

Rural development matters for the whole country, because in 1961, 82% of India's population resided in villages and in 1971 the percentage was 80.01%. So far the rural area has shouldered the responsibility of providing food grains and other raw material to urban areas, supplying labour to the industrial sectors of the city and taking care of natural resources. There are three major challenges with reference to rural development, namely, bringing about economic development, developing facilities to meet social needs, and finally bringing about a change of attitude in matters concerning society, culture and ways of thinking. It is equally necessary to expedite irrigation projects and to bring about land reforms. Among the social needs, priority has to be given to facilities for public hygiene and health-care, because even today the rural population faces problems related to the year round provision of drinking water, toilets, open drainage, narrow roads, inadequate electrification and a lack of facilities for medical treatment. There is also a lack of good quality educational facilities from the primary level to higher education, and of centres for recreation and libraries. Electricity is a further need, since automatic pumps are required to water the fields and electricity is needed to preserve perishable food items such as milk, eggs, fruits and vegetables, to run fertiliser projects and to provide lights for studying at night. The unavailability of means of livelihood in rural areas also drives people to migrate to the cities, so jobs have to be made available in villages and a balance has to be achieved in economic development. That is why it is necessary to give special attention to rural areas.

The Constitution of India states that the primary duty of the government is to raise the people's standard of living, to ensure proper nutrition and to improve public health, and the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare at the Centre helps the state governments in this regard. Making primary health services as well as medical care available to rural people, the tribals and the poor was an objective of the Sixth Five Year plan, and recognition was given to Unani, Homoeopathy, Ayurveda and Naturopathy in addition to Allopathy. In 1962, the first successful open heart surgery was performed under the leadership of Dr N. Gopinath at the Christian Medical College Hospital at Vellore in Tamil Nadu, so it is no longer necessary to go abroad for such treatment. The invention of the 'Jaipur Foot' transformed the lives of the disabled, who before 1968 had to suffer for the rest of their lives after losing a leg; Dr Pramod Sethi made these artificial limbs with the help of the craftsman Ramchandra Sharma. Kidney transplants were not common in India till 1971, but in that year Dr Johny and Dr Mohan Rao successfully performed one at the same hospital at Vellore, and nowadays patients from underdeveloped countries come to India for such surgeries. Since 1978, the support of 'test-tube baby' technology has been available to childless couples; this first successful attempt at artificial conception was carried out at Kolkata under the supervision of Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyaya, and a girl named Durga was born. Before 1978, six out of every ten Indian infants born each year faced fatal health problems in their very first year, so an immunisation programme was taken up against polio, measles, tetanus, TB, diphtheria and whooping cough, and the 'pulse polio' programme started in 1995 has controlled polio. Because of this progress in the medical field, the life of Indians has become relatively free of health concerns.
